sourceText: cells: Ic, Ai Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the WATTS-BLINDSIGHT-LAB sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. A species solves problems and manipulates adversaries without signs of subjective experience. The memorial bore the name of Peter Watts — Blindsight precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The problem of identity was not a word game. In worlds where a mind could be copied or distributed, inheritance, guilt, contract, and mourning depended on the answer. Vela tracked the differences erased by elegant explanations. For her, two worlds that produced the same statistic did not thereby become the same world. At the center of the conflict was Miro, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. 167 The problem closed quickly around them: Aster sees the possibility of eliminating her Hunger by eliminating the conscious part that suffers, and Marae forces her to admit the temptation. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ic — Intelligence without Consciousness: performance does not imply subjective experience; Ai — Artificial Intelligence: an artificial agent becomes a moral and social actor. Course references included Peter Watts — Blindsight; AI fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Marae broke the first consensus. ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ Vela answered without raising their voice: ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 168 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. The children discover that an optimization radical enough can cure the problem by eliminating the patient. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the ALTERATION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a 169 body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 170 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
